paras: The attempted lynching of Harry and Courtland Gordon was a failed attempt by a mob to take the two brothers from the jail at Vincennes, Indiana, and hang them in early 1882, after their arrest on a charge of robbing and maltreating an aged couple. The sheriff stopped the mob, and the brothers were later tried and found guilty, after which a third brother claimed that he and an uncle had committed the crime.

Harry and Courtland Gordon were arrested at Vincennes, Ind., charged with robbing and maltreating an elderly couple. The coverage names neither the couple nor the date of the robbery, and it does not state the race of the brothers.

While the brothers were held, a mob tried to take them out of jail to hang them but, in the words of one report, "were baffled by a plucky Sheriff." No date, time, crowd size or further detail of the attempt appears in the coverage.

The brothers were tried and found guilty in mid-April 1882. Their brother Joe then declared that he and an uncle were "the guilty ones," saying he had meant to stay silent if his brothers were acquitted but would not let them go to the State Prison. He also said he had been present at the attempted lynching and would have spoken out then if it had been necessary. No report of what followed his statement was found.

The only account found ran on April 20, 1882, in the Helena Weekly Herald of Montana, as an unheadlined paragraph in a column of miscellany between an editorial on Chinese immigration and a note on Longfellow. The item treated the mob attempt as a brief prelude, praised the "plucky" sheriff, and gave most of its space to the brother's late confession.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob tried to take the two prisoners from jail to hang them and was stopped by the sheriff (A2).
No one was killed: the mob that tried to take the Gordons from jail to hang them over a robbery charge was 'baffled' by the sheriff, and both men were later tried (A2). It was an attempted lynching.
Only one brief, in a Montana paper of 1882-04-20, describes the episode (A2); the other linked article is not about it (A1).
